title: Internet Calendaring and Scheduling Core Object Specification (iCalendar)
subtitle: The plain-text format behind every calendar invite and .ics file.
summary: iCalendar defines a text format, labelled text/calendar, for exchanging events, to-dos, journal entries, free/busy time and time zones between calendar programs. Information is written as folded lines of NAME:value pairs, grouped into components such as VEVENT between BEGIN and END markers. It replaced RFC 2445 in 2009 and is the format behind .ics files and calendar invitations.

plainLanguage.summary: iCalendar is a text format, labelled text/calendar, for exchanging events, to-dos, journal entries, free/busy time and time zones between calendar programs. Data is written as folded NAME:value lines grouped into components such as VEVENT. It replaced RFC 2445 in 2009 and underlies .ics files and calendar invitations.

tldr.problem: Calendar programs from different vendors stored events in private formats, so sharing a meeting between them was unreliable.
tldr.mechanism: A UTF-8 text format of content lines (NAME;PARAM=x:value) nested in components such as VCALENDAR, VEVENT and VALARM, with a formal ABNF grammar and a recurrence-rule mini-language.
tldr.outcome: Nearly every calendar app can import and export .ics files and send invitations as text/calendar, which makes this the base of calendar interoperability.

today: iCalendar is everywhere calendars are shared. Files ending in .ics are iCalendar objects, calendar invitations in email carry them as text/calendar parts, and subscription feeds for holidays, sports fixtures and conference schedules are served in this format. CalDAV (RFC 4791) stores and syncs calendars as iCalendar objects. Later RFCs have extended rather than replaced it, for example adding new properties in RFC 7986.

implementations.note: All import and export .ics files and send invitations as iCalendar.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The use of calendaring and scheduling had grown to the point where businesses depended on it, but different programs could not exchange the information. RFC 5545 defines the Internet Calendaring and Scheduling Core Object Specification, or iCalendar, as a MIME content type for exchanging events, to-dos, journal entries and free/busy time.

The object is deliberately independent of transport. The RFC lists SMTP, HTTP, a file system, a clipboard or drag and drop, and even infrared as ways to carry it. It also provides for methods that map the content type onto requests, replies and cancellations, but the scheduling protocol that uses them is defined elsewhere, in iTIP (RFC 5546).

The format comes with a formal grammar in ABNF (RFC 5234). The RFC says this grammar is required for parser implementers and is the definitive reference where the prose is ambiguous.
sections.plainLanguage: Different calendar programs could not exchange information, even though businesses depended on scheduling. iCalendar is a standard format for events, to-dos, journal entries and free/busy time. It does not depend on how it is carried, so SMTP, HTTP or a plain file can all be used.

sections.title: Content lines and folding
sections.content:
Everything in an iCalendar object is a content line, ending in CRLF. The general form is a name, optional ;PARAM=value parameters, a colon and then the value. Names, parameter names and enumerated values are case-insensitive; other values are case-sensitive unless stated.

Lines SHOULD NOT be longer than 75 octets, excluding the line break. A longer line is folded by inserting a CRLF followed by a single space or tab. A parser must unfold first, removing each CRLF plus the one whitespace character after it, before looking at the line's meaning.

The 75 limit is counted in octets, not characters. The RFC warns that simple implementations sometimes fold in the middle of a UTF-8 multi-octet sequence, so unfolding must restore the original bytes before they are decoded.

Values containing a colon, semicolon or comma inside a parameter must be placed in quoted text. Multi-valued items are separated by commas within one line, or by repeating the property on separate lines.
sections.plainLanguage: Every line is a name, optional ;PARAM=value parameters, a colon and a value. Lines should not exceed 75 octets (bytes). Longer lines are folded by inserting a line break and one space. A parser must undo this folding before reading the line.

sections.title: Objects and components
sections.content:
An iCalendar object starts with BEGIN:VCALENDAR and ends with END:VCALENDAR. A stream may hold one or more such objects one after another. Inside are calendar properties that apply to the whole object, then one or more components.

An object MUST include the PRODID and VERSION properties and at least one component. VERSION is 2.0 for this specification. The RFC defines six component types.

VEVENT
A scheduled amount of time, such as a meeting; also used for anniversaries and all-day events.
VTODO
A task, which can have a due date and a percent complete.
VJOURNAL
A dated journal or note entry.
VFREEBUSY
Published busy time, or a request or reply about it.
VTIMEZONE
The rules for a time zone, including standard and daylight offsets.
VALARM
A reminder. It can only appear inside a VEVENT or VTODO.

Unrecognised components of the experimental X- form or registered by IANA must be ignored, but applications that import iCalendar objects SHOULD support all the component types in the RFC and SHOULD NOT silently drop any component, as that can lose user data.
sections.plainLanguage: An iCalendar object starts with BEGIN:VCALENDAR and ends with END:VCALENDAR. It must include PRODID and VERSION and at least one component. The six components are VEVENT (an event), VTODO (a task), VJOURNAL, VFREEBUSY, VTIMEZONE and VALARM (a reminder).

sections.title: Events, to-dos and identity
sections.content:
A VEVENT must have DTSTAMP and UID. DTSTART is required too, unless the object has a METHOD property. The UID is a persistent, globally unique identifier; it is what lets a program recognise an update to an event it already knows about, together with SEQUENCE for revisions.

DTEND is the non-inclusive end of the event. An event may use DTEND or DURATION but not both. If DTSTART is a DATE with neither, the event lasts one day; this is how all-day events are written. Where DTSTART is a DATE-TIME with no end, the event ends at the same moment it starts.

Appendix A of the RFC says that the value type of DTEND or DUE must match that of DTSTART. A date-only start with a date-time end is not valid.

Reminders are VALARM components nested inside. Each needs an ACTION (AUDIO, DISPLAY or EMAIL) and a TRIGGER, either a duration relative to the start or end, such as -PT30M, or an absolute UTC time.
sections.plainLanguage: Every event has a UID, a globally unique and persistent identifier. A program uses the UID, together with SEQUENCE for revisions, to recognize an update to an event it already has. An event ends at DTEND or after a DURATION, but not both. A date-only start with no end is a one-day event.

sections.title: Dates, times and time zones
sections.content:
A DATE-TIME value can take three forms. Floating time has no suffix and no zone, such as 19980118T230000; it means the same wall-clock time wherever the viewer is, which suits "lunch at noon every day". UTC time ends in Z, such as 19980119T070000Z. Local time with a zone uses the TZID parameter, such as TZID=America/New_York:19980119T020000. The form with a UTC offset, like -0800, MUST NOT be used.

A TZID parameter must not be applied to a UTC time. When the local time occurs twice, in the autumn shift, the first occurrence is meant; when it falls in a gap, the offset before the gap is used.

Time zones are described by VTIMEZONE components, each with a TZID and STANDARD and DAYLIGHT sub-components giving TZOFFSETFROM, TZOFFSETTO and usually a recurrence rule for the changeover. The RFC says a VTIMEZONE must be included for each distinct TZID that is used in the object.
sections.plainLanguage: A date-time can be floating (no zone, the same wall-clock time everywhere), UTC (ending in Z), or local time with a TZID time zone name. The UTC offset form, like -0800, must not be used. Time zones are described by VTIMEZONE components with standard and daylight rules.

sections.title: Recurrence rules
sections.content:
The RECUR value type, used by RRULE, is a short language of NAME=VALUE parts separated by semicolons. Only FREQ is required, with a value from SECONDLY up to YEARLY, and for compatibility with older software it must be written first. INTERVAL sets the step, defaulting to 1. The rule ends with UNTIL or COUNT, which may not both appear; with neither, it repeats forever.

Parts such as BYMONTH, BYDAY, BYMONTHDAY and BYSETPOS narrow or expand which occurrences within each period are chosen. A day prefixed with a number picks the nth one, so -1MO is the last Monday of the month. For example, FREQ=MONTHLY;BYDAY=MO,TU,WE,TH,FR;BYSETPOS=-1 gives the last working day of every month.

The first occurrence is always DTSTART, which counts toward COUNT. Extra dates are added with RDATE and removed with EXDATE. A changed single instance is a separate component with a RECURRENCE-ID that points at the occurrence it replaces.
sections.plainLanguage: A recurrence rule (RRULE) describes repeating events in one line of NAME=VALUE parts. Only FREQ is required, such as WEEKLY or MONTHLY. Other parts set the step, the end (UNTIL or COUNT) and which days count. For example, -1MO means the last Monday of the month.

sections.title: Media type and security
sections.content:
Section 8.1 registers the media type text/calendar. It has optional parameters charset, method, component and optinfo. UTF-8 is the charset this revision supports, other charsets are deprecated, and parsers MUST accept UTF-8 or US-ASCII. When every object in a stream shares one METHOD value, the method parameter must be set to match it.

The Security Considerations section is short because this RFC only defines a data format. Calendar data is privacy-sensitive, so the transport should resist eavesdropping, replay, message insertion, deletion, modification and man-in-the-middle attacks. The RFC leaves the details to the protocols that carry it, naming iTIP, iMIP and CalDAV (RFC 4791).
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC registers the media type text/calendar, so programs can recognize the content. UTF-8 is the supported character set. Calendar data is privacy-sensitive, so the transport should resist eavesdropping and tampering. The RFC leaves those details to the protocols that carry it.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 2445
sections.content:
RFC 5545 obsoletes RFC 2445, the 1998 original. It did not change the format's basic shape. Its Appendix A lists the new restrictions, the restrictions removed and the deprecated features.

It added restrictions such as DTSTART SHOULD be synchronized with the recurrence rule and BYHOUR, BYMINUTE and BYSECOND MUST NOT be used when DTSTART is a DATE. It deprecated EXRULE, the THISANDPRIOR value of RANGE, and the PROCEDURE action. DURATION can no longer appear in a VFREEBUSY.

It has itself been updated several times by later RFCs, which add properties, relationships and alarm features.
sections.plainLanguage: RFC 5545 replaces the 1998 RFC 2445 without changing the format's basic shape. It clarifies unclear rules, adds some restrictions, and deprecates a few features, such as EXRULE. Later RFCs have updated it further.
